What The Chip Happened To AI & Semiconductor Investors Today?

1) NVIDIA $NVDA / Microsoft $MSFT: Microsoft opened preorders for Surface Laptop Ultra and Surface RTX Spark Dev Box, both built around NVIDIA RTX Spark N1X. The U.S. store lists the entry laptop at $2,599.99 with 24GB unified memory and a 512GB SSD; availability begins October 16. The $5,999.99 Dev Box has 128GB memory and a 2TB SSD, with U.S. shipments planned for November. Alongside the hardware, Microsoft made Execution Containers generally available, letting developers define agent access to files and networks outside the agent’s control.

2) AMD $AMD / Samsung $SSNLF: Lisa Su met Samsung’s semiconductor leadership in Seoul for just over three hours, including dinner, according to Edaily. During the visit, she described tight memory supply, encouraged capacity expansion and discussed planning three to five years ahead. The product connection predates this meeting: Samsung’s March 18 memorandum of understanding (MOU) with AMD outlined primary HBM4 supply for MI455X GPUs and collaboration on advanced DRAM and optimized DDR5 for sixth-generation EPYC “Venice” CPUs and Helios racks, following HBM3E supply for MI350X and MI355X. Foundry cooperation was an opportunity for discussion in that MOU; Edaily’s completed-meeting report disclosed no specific progress toward a foundry deal.

3) Google $GOOGL / Unity $U: Google launched Playground, an experimental browser platform that lets users describe a game, play it and refine it through conversation, then share it by link or through an Explore gallery. It is available to U.S. users aged 18 and over, with creation access rolling out in tiers tied to Google AI subscription. Unity’s Spark integration is forthcoming, with testing underway and a closed beta coming soon. Google describes richer mechanics, 3D capabilities and Unity runtime flexibility; Unity says Spark connects directly to its Asset Store. The intended audience includes people with a game idea but no development experience, alongside artists and modders. That expands the creation approach beyond Unity’s May beta Editor tools for Unity 6+ projects, which helped developers write scripts, change scenes and verify behavior.

4) Wolfspeed $WOLF: The company announced a conditional loan commitment of up to $1.5B from the U.S. Department of War’s Office of Strategic Capital to support domestic silicon carbide materials and wide bandgap power devices. Planned uses include upgrading gallium nitride epitaxy for communications and electronic-warfare systems and developing radiation-hardening capabilities. The contemplated facility is senior secured, allows delayed draws and has a 30-year term. Subject to definitive agreements, Wolfspeed would issue VWAP-based warrants for up to 7.5% of fully diluted equity, pro rata as financing tranches are funded. Funding remains subject to due diligence, agreements, government approvals, appropriations and third-party consents; Wolfspeed says financing is not assured.

5) Samsung HBM4E: Samsung’s 12-high HBM4E reportedly passed qualification at NVIDIA and major hyperscalers in late September, according to Hankyung. Samsung told the publication it could not confirm the report. The prior confirmed step was its May 29 announcement of sample shipments: 48GB capacity and bandwidth of up to 3.6TB/s per stack. Hankyung’s reported milestone is a qualification pass, while customer-specific volumes and mass-production timing remain unconfirmed. Samsung’s July earnings update separately said HBM4 sales had scaled during the second quarter and projected that AI/server-memory demand would keep the market undersupplied in the second half.

6) Aehr Test Systems $AEHR: Aehr’s October 7 announcement reported about $6M in follow-on Sonoma production orders for its lead hyperscale customer’s next-generation AI processor. The order includes systems, burn-in modules, device-specific sockets and software enhancements, with deliveries to a Taiwan outsourced assembly and test partner scheduled over the next six months. Aehr says the customer’s first Sonoma processor is already in high-volume production; its second program is expected to ramp in calendar 2027, with eventual volumes expected to exceed the first. The initial production win for that next-generation processor was announced February 11. Sonoma provides independent thermal control across zones within these high-power packages. For company-wide context, Aehr’s July 14 outlook projected $130–150M of revenue for the fiscal year ending June 25, 2027, versus $50M of revenue in FY2026 ended May 29, 2026.

7) CoreWeave $CRWV: CoreWeave’s October 7 India announcement outlined a planned 240 MW AI cloud deployment with AdaniConneX at Taloja in Navi Mumbai. The campus would span three 80 MW buildings, with CoreWeave as sole tenant, and the company plans to install NVIDIA Vera Rubin. The first phase is expected in mid-2028, followed by additional capacity in stages; a further expansion of up to 240 MW is a separate opportunity. The design includes direct liquid cooling and non-evaporative chilled water. This follows CoreWeave’s August 4 Indonesia expansion announcement: three facilities totaling 360 MW of contracted IT power, expected to become operational in 2028.

【10/8話題】コインチェックがNAC取扱開始、NOT A HOTEL DAOはCoincheck CaaS導入、Samsung WalletでUSDC国際送金を提供へなど（音声ニュース）
WebX STUDIO【仮想通貨 ブロックチェーン総合番組】　#AI要約

暗号資産市場で進む決済・規制対応とブロックチェーン活用

🔳NOT A HOTEL COINの取り扱い開始
コインチェックがNOT A HOTEL COINの取り扱いを開始し、国内での取り扱いはGMOコインに続く2例目となった。コインチェックで売買できる暗号資産は36銘柄となった。

🔳NOT A HOTELとのサービス連携
コインチェックの組み込み型金融サービスを活用し、NOT A HOTELアプリから保有するNOT A HOTEL COINの残高確認やレンディングなどが利用できるようになった。

🔳宿泊権と暗号資産を連携
NOT A HOTEL COINを貸し出して宿泊権を得る仕組みや、保有数量と期間に応じて当選確率が高まる宿泊権抽選、管理費や飲食などへの支払いに利用できる仕組みが紹介された。

🔳NOT A HOTEL COINのこれまで
NOT A HOTEL COINは2024年にGMOコインでIEOを実施し、20億円を調達した暗号資産で、今回のコインチェック対応によって利用環境が広がった。

🔳Samsung WalletでUSDC送金
Samsungは米国でSamsung WalletにUSDCの保有と国際送金機能を導入する予定で、別の暗号資産アプリを導入せずにステーブルコインを利用できるようにする。

🔳銀行口座への国際送金
Samsung Walletでは外部ウォレットだけでなく60カ国超の対象銀行口座への送金にも対応し、受取人は暗号資産ウォレットを用意せず現地通貨で受け取れる仕組みになる。

🔳SuiとSolanaへの対応
Samsung WalletではSolanaやSui上のUSDCに対応し、Suiではネットワーク手数料なしでUSDCを送金できる仕組みも提供されると説明された。

🔳BitMineのイーサリアム戦略
BitMineはイーサリアム供給量の5%保有を財務戦略の目標としており、目標に到達した段階で追加購入を終了する方針を示した。

🔳イーサリアムの大量保有
BitMineは約15カ月で約600万ETHを取得し、目標とする供給量の5%に近づいているとしており、保有するETHの約84%をステーキングに充てている。

🔳Suiの高速処理実験
Suiのオフチェーン技術Sui Tunnelsを使った公開実験で毎秒約4061万件の処理を記録し、当初目標だった毎秒2000万件の約2倍となった。

🔳AIエージェント向け処理基盤
Sui TunnelsはAIエージェント同士による大量の決済やサービス利用を想定し、処理をオフチェーンで実行して最終結果をSuiメインネットで確定する仕組みとして紹介された。

🔳Suiの記録に関する注意点
毎秒約4061万件という数字はSui Tunnels内部で測定されたものであり、Suiメインネット自体が同じ処理性能を持つことを示す数字ではないと説明された。

🔳カルダノの規制対応トークン規格
カルダノではCIP-0113がメインネットで利用可能となり、ステーブルコインやトークン化された金融商品などに本人確認、制裁確認、移転制限、凍結などの規則を組み込めるようになった。

🔳金融機関によるトークン活用
CIP-0113ではKYCやAMLなどの条件を満たした相手だけに資産を移転できるようにするなど、規制対象の金融資産をブロックチェーン上で管理しやすくする仕組みが導入された。

🔳金融庁が無登録業者を一覧化
金融庁は無登録で暗号資産交換業を行ったとして過去に警告した業者の一覧ページを公開し、国内3件、海外など22件の情報を掲載した。

🔳無登録業者への注意喚起
金融庁は無登録業者について顧客資産の管理やシステム、トラブル対応などを確認できないとして、取引前に登録状況や警告履歴を確認するよう呼びかけている。

🔳Polygonの決済基盤がTron対応
Polygon Labsの企業向け決済基盤Polygon Open Money StackがTronに対応し、Tron上のUSDTと法定通貨の交換、ウォレット管理、銀行入出金などをまとめて利用できるようになった。

🔳Tron上のUSDT市場
Tronでは940億ドルを超えるUSDTが流通しており、全ブロックチェーン上のUSDT供給量の半分以上を占めると説明された。

🔳ステーブルコインと銀行決済を接続
企業はTron上で受け取ったUSDTを現地通貨へ交換して銀行口座へ送金するなど、ブロックチェーンと既存の金融インフラをつないだサービスを構築しやすくなる。

🔳クロスチェーン送金にも対応
Polygonの仕組みではTron上のUSDTをEthereumなど別のブロックチェーン上の資産へ交換して送金する処理も可能で、利用者がブリッジを直接操作する必要を減らせる。

🔳暗号資産の実利用が拡大
今回のニュースでは、宿泊、国際送金、企業決済、金融商品のトークン化、AIエージェント間取引など、暗号資産やブロックチェーンを実際のサービスへ組み込む動きが広がっていることが示された。

GLOBAL AI ANALYSIS REPORT — MIDDAY INTELLIGENCE
By Ed Hernandez | KEYSTONE PULSE MEDIA / Global Media Center
Thursday, October 8, 2026

Executive Midday Pulse — The Interface Break Edition

THE INTERFACE BREAK: Chat just became software. GPT-6 and Intelligent UI reached every ChatGPT tier this morning — buttons, charts, calculators inline — while Anthropic’s Haiku 5.5 landed up to 90% cheaper and Samsung guided a record 107.4 trillion won (~$80B) Q3 operating profit on HBM. 

→ OpenAI says the Free and Go rollout covers 1.2B weekly users; paid tiers started Oct 7 on GPT-6 Sol, free tiers Oct 8 on Luna. 
→ Haiku 5.5: $0.10 / $0.50 per million tokens under 100k, effort controls, 72.4% on OSWorld 2.1 in Anthropic’s tests; Sonnet 5.5 cache reads halved. 
→ Samsung: first tech firm to clear 100 trillion won quarterly profit; HBM4 now shipping into the Vera Rubin ramp. Shortage talk extends into 2028. 
→ Broadcom is arranging $50B+ to finance OpenAI’s custom chips; Oracle and SpaceX are in parallel chip-debt talks. 
→ Asia-Pacific: AirTrunk maps up to $30B in Japan data centers; NVIDIA’s Australia partners still target ~2 GW of DSX factories by 2027. 
→ DeepSeek’s V4.1-Flash holds the China coding lane ahead of a reported $12B+ raise; Mistral Large 4 (1T, open weights due late October) is Europe’s answer. 

Arena closed a $200M Series B at roughly $3.1B and, in the same breath, shipped the Alignment Index — the first behavioral benchmark built at real scale. Not a capability test. A behavior test. 

The numbers: 

→ 90,000+ agent sessions across 27 models 
→ Three failure signals scored: unauthorized action, false attribution, deceptive completion 
→ GPT-6.1 Sol leads at 87.9 · Claude Opus 5.5 at 83.2 · Grok 4.7 at 82.7

The last six hours did not crown a new frontier model. They repriced the stack underneath one. Intelligence is being unbundled into a cheap agent layer (Haiku, Luna, Flash) and a capital layer (HBM4, custom XPUs, gigawatt shells). Whoever owns the interface — not the parameter count — captures the next billion users. Memory, not models, is the binding constraint.

Is the chat box already obsolete in your workflow, or is Intelligent UI still a demo?

■観測者ZERO 現時点での総括

観測者ZEROは、米国株は半導体を中心に戻り売りが優勢とみる。米半導体株指数（SOX）は3.75%安まで下げ、NASDAQ総合も1%を超える下落となった。寄り付き後の下げ渋りより、その後に安値圏へ押し戻された事実を重く見る。

原油高と高い金利水準が続く間は、成長期待だけで半導体株を買い直す勢いは限られそうだ。ただしSOXが当日の始値12,842.8ポイントを回復して保ち、NASDAQも始値27,416.03ポイントを取り戻すなら、売りが一巡したとの見方に改める。
その場合は前日終値への戻りを試すかが焦点となる。この判断の対象は、日本時間9日午前5時の通常取引終了までとする。

records.text:
META: THE CONSUMER-AGENT OPPORTUNITY REQUIRES A DIFFERENT MONETIZATION MODEL

Meta's consumer-agent thesis is strategically significant because it combines distribution, consumer engagement, transaction discovery, and potential workflow execution. The product transition is substantive. Meta's Muse announcement describes a persistent cloud computer that can continue working after the application closes, use connected services, and complete approved actions. These capabilities expand the opportunity beyond conversational engagement.

Coatue estimates roughly 7 million US Muse downloads during approximately the first 27 days. That supports rapid initial acquisition within the source's methodology. It does not establish retained users, completed tasks, paying adoption, contribution margins, or the strength of the product relative to mature competitors. Comparisons with other applications' launch cohorts also involve different distribution conditions, calendar periods, and pre-existing brand reach.

The advertising scenario is ambitious but not mathematically implausible. Increasing annual advertising revenue per daily active user from an estimated $68 in 2026 to $153 in 2031 represents a 125% increase and approximately 17.6% annual growth. The footnote attributes the outcome to greater time spent, some ad-load growth, and better pricing through improved targeting. A complete model would need to specify each contribution, maintain a consistent active-user denominator, and separate Muse's incremental effect from developments in the existing advertising business.

The most material qualification comes from Meta itself. The current Muse announcement states that users' conversations and data in their virtual machines are not shared with Meta's advertising systems. The deck's proposed shift toward targeting based on messages, emails, shopping, and transactions therefore cannot be modeled as an unrestricted current flow of private agent data into advertising. Other permitted signals and engagement improvements may still benefit monetization, but that requires a separately specified mechanism.

This restriction also has a potentially positive strategic effect. Strong privacy commitments may encourage users to connect sensitive accounts and delegate more valuable tasks. Improved trust can support adoption and retention while limiting the most direct advertising monetization route. Product success and advertising uplift can consequently occur on different timelines.

The commerce calculation requires a further distinction between the industry opportunity and Meta's achievable revenue. The assumptions are $21 trillion of global retail sales excluding China in 2031, 40% e-commerce penetration, 30% agent-mediated penetration, and a 10% agent take rate. Multiplication produces approximately $252 billion, rounded to $250 billion. That is an ecosystem revenue pool before applying Meta's share.

The sensitivity to take rate and share is substantial. Keeping the same underlying transaction volume but assuming a 3% realized take rate and a 25% Meta share produces approximately $18.9 billion of annual revenue. This is an illustrative sensitivity rather than a forecast. It shows why the $250 billion headline cannot be treated as a Meta revenue estimate.

Current commercial terms also do not establish the assumed fee. Shopify's documentation for direct checkout on Meta surfaces, including Muse when available, states that merchants pay standard payment-processing fees without an additional selling fee for that checkout. This applies to a particular channel and does not determine all future monetization. It does establish that a general 10% agent commission is a scenario assumption rather than an observed channel-wide rate.

A high agent take rate would need to be supported by incremental merchant economics. Merchants already fund advertising, payments, fulfillment, returns, discounts, and other distribution costs. An additional commission is attractive when agents generate purchases that would not otherwise occur, improve conversion, or lower other acquisition expenses. If the commission replaces existing advertising expenditure, the result may be a redistribution of the same transaction economics rather than a fully incremental profit pool.

Advertising and commerce estimates should therefore not be added without assessing substitution. The strongest bullish outcome would combine higher purchase frequency, better conversion, lower customer-acquisition costs, and a durable share of those improvements accruing to Meta. The principal downside is that consumer utility expands quickly while competitive checkout options and operating costs constrain monetization.

The decisive indicators are retained active agents, valuable tasks completed, approved integrations, purchase conversion, repeat transaction behavior, and contribution profit per active user. Download growth is an initial distribution signal; these operating measures determine the economic value of the franchise.

AGENTIC CPUs: A SUPPORTED CATEGORY EXPANSION WITH AN INCOMPLETE INTEL CAPTURE MODEL

Coatue's agentic CPU thesis identifies an important source of incremental demand. Agents execute code, run browsers, retrieve data, coordinate workflows, and invoke existing enterprise services. These activities can expand CPU requirements alongside accelerator inference.

The headline calculation is highly assumption-dependent. Dividing 8 billion agents by 64 agents per server CPU produces approximately 125 million CPUs. At a $10,000 average selling price, the cumulative opportunity is $1.25 trillion. Dividing by a 5-year life produces approximately $250 billion annually. The slide adds approximately $50 billion of non-agentic demand to show a $300 billion total server CPU market in 2031.

The footnote materially narrows this claim. The $250 billion figure is a simple annualization, deployment is weighted toward 2031, and the detailed forecast uses an approximately $8,300 ASP in 2031 rather than the $10,000 headline assumption. Annualizing a cumulative fleet requirement does not independently establish shipments or revenue in a particular year. Annual sales depend on deployment timing, replacement cohorts, hardware life, and changes in capacity per processor.

The largest uncertainty is the relationship between an agent and the computing resources it actually consumes. A persistent agent can spend substantial time waiting, while a smaller number of continuously active agents may generate intensive workloads. Idle state can consume memory and storage without requiring equivalent CPU execution. Concurrency, task frequency, CPU time per task, memory capacity, and service-level requirements are therefore essential variables.

The density assumption alone has large consequences. Increasing supported agents per CPU from 64 to 128 halves the modeled equipment requirement with all other assumptions unchanged. This does not reduce the amount of useful work being performed. It demonstrates how improvements in server efficiency can expand the agent economy while limiting processor unit growth.

Primary industry evidence supports the category while reinforcing this qualification. AMD's July EPYC launch identifies separate CPU roles in agent execution, accelerator support, and enterprise services. Its methodology explicitly describes agent counts as theoretical estimates based on available CPU threads and states that actual capacity varies with workload, memory, software, orchestration, and configuration. There is no universal conversion from agent count to CPU demand.

Intel is participating in the demand expansion. Its Q2 disclosures reported DCAI revenue of $6.3 billion, up 59% year over year, with approximately $2.5 billion of segment operating profit. Management described server demand exceeding available supply. However, Intel Foundry also reported a $2.1 billion operating loss. The equity thesis therefore depends on consolidated manufacturing economics and capital requirements in addition to server-market growth.

The opportunity is also contested. Arm's agentic CPU announcement identifies Meta as lead partner and co-developer across multiple generations. That relationship is directly relevant to the deck's juxtaposition of a Meta consumer-agent thesis and an Intel CPU thesis: growth in Meta's agent infrastructure does not automatically translate into Intel share. AMD, Arm-based designs, and customer-developed architectures provide alternative supply paths.

The supported conclusion is that agentic computing can materially expand CPU demand. The security-specific conclusion requires separate forecasts for active workload intensity, processor density, industry shipments, realized pricing, supplier share, and consolidated cash returns.

CAPITAL SPENDING: LARGE REQUIREMENTS, UNEVEN DEFINITIONS, AND PHYSICAL CONSTRAINTS

The $2.8 trillion estimate for 2028 AI capital expenditure is among the presentation's most consequential assumptions. Its scale would make infrastructure financing a major determinant of the industry's trajectory. However, the comparison with other capital pools mixes expenditure categories, periods, and geographies. Using the displayed $2.1 trillion mortgage-origination figure produces approximately 1.33x, rather than the slide's roughly 1.5x comparison. More fundamentally, mortgage originations are financing flows, whereas capital expenditure measures investment in assets.

The historical investment-intensity comparison also requires adjustment. Slide 22 compares domestic historical investment with global AI investment divided by US GDP. Its approximately 2.9% figure is therefore not a directly comparable measure of domestic US investment intensity. The chart conveys scale relative to a familiar denominator, but it does not establish that US AI investment has surpassed earlier domestic infrastructure booms on a consistent basis.

A credible aggregate spending model must distinguish equipment purchases, facility construction, compute-service commitments, capital raised, and revenue recognized. The same infrastructure can generate all of these figures. Adding them indiscriminately would count the underlying investment repeatedly. Capacity estimates require similar discipline because customers, operators, landlords, and vendors can refer to the same campus.

OpenAI's PORTS-Pike announcement provides a concrete example. The agreement covers approximately 8 GW of IT capacity, with buildout extending through 2032 and the first 800 MW expected in 2028. SB Energy will build, own, and operate the campus under a 20-year lease, with OpenAI paying as completed capacity becomes available. The difference between announced capacity and initial delivered capacity is therefore substantial.

Coatue's compute-equity scenario assumes approximately 222.5 GW of incremental capacity during 2025–2031. At an illustrative 80% average draw, that capacity would consume approximately 1,560 TWh annually before additional facility overhead if the capacity figure represents IT load. This is a physical sensitivity, not an independent demand forecast. It illustrates the importance of generation, transmission, interconnection, construction, and commissioning schedules.

The binding constraint can also change by location and period. Available funding does not ensure available power; available power does not ensure completed facilities; and completed facilities do not ensure fully utilized equipment. Delays can leave interest accruing before revenue begins and can expose hardware to technological aging before it reaches its intended utilization.

Consequently, financed, energized, revenue-producing capacity is a more informative measure than the sum of announced projects. Power and cooling suppliers may benefit from physical bottlenecks, but even those exposures depend on funded execution and the timing of actual installations.

FINANCING: EQUITY REQUIREMENTS ARE HIGHLY SENSITIVE TO LENDING TERMS

Coatue assumes approximately $40 billion of compute equipment per GW, financed with $30 billion of debt and $10 billion of equity. Applying the $10 billion equity requirement to 222.5 GW produces approximately $2.225 trillion. The footnote explicitly states that this is not an unmet third-party financing gap. Internally generated cash, retained earnings, sponsor capital, existing commitments, and customer prepayments can fund portions of the requirement.

The estimate also excludes the financing mix for an additional $10 billion–$15 billion per GW of buildings and power infrastructure. These long-lived assets require separate capital and have different collateral characteristics from computing equipment. Treating the entire complex as a uniform financing asset obscures differences in useful life, cash-flow durability, and residual value.

The leverage sensitivity is substantial. Reducing equipment loan-to-value from 75% to 65% raises required equity per GW from $10 billion to $14 billion, an increase of 40%. Across the modeled capacity, the additional equity requirement is approximately $890 billion. A moderate tightening in lending terms can therefore create a much larger percentage change in required shareholder capital.

Financing cost also matters. A 200-basis-point increase on $30 billion of debt adds approximately $600 million of annual interest per GW, equivalent to 6% of the initial $10 billion equity contribution before taxes or other effects. These are illustrative sensitivities, but they show why growth can remain strong while equity returns deteriorate.

Residual-value risk is similarly amplified. Before amortization, a 25% decline in the value of $40 billion of equipment eliminates the original $10 billion equity cushion against $30 billion of debt. Durable contracted cash flows can protect lenders and investors from immediate asset-price movements, but that protection depends on customer creditworthiness, enforceability, service delivery, contract duration, and termination provisions.

Off-balance-sheet ownership does not eliminate these exposures. In Meta's Hyperion structure, Blue Owl-managed funds own 80% of the venture and Meta owns 20%. The approximately $27 billion development budget concerns buildings and long-lived infrastructure. Meta leases the facilities and provides a capped residual-value guarantee covering the first 16 years of operations. The structure creates financing flexibility while retaining contingent economic exposure.

Accounting classifications can also change reported investment without changing the underlying plan. Microsoft disclosed that extending estimated building lives would shift more future data-center leases from finance leases to operating leases, reducing reported capital expenditure expectations while leaving underlying calendar-year investment expectations unchanged apart from that classification effect. Lower reported capex therefore does not necessarily indicate weaker infrastructure demand or reduced economic commitments.

CoreWeave provides direct evidence of the funding challenge. Its June 2026 filing reported $103.7 billion of remaining performance obligations and $35.6 billion of debt principal. During the first half, operating cash flow of $3.7 billion compared with $14.1 billion of cash purchases of property and equipment, leaving a calculated gap of approximately $10.5 billion before financing and other investing flows. Contracted revenue visibility does not remove the need to fund delivery.

Its reported profitability measures demonstrate the distinction between operating activity and shareholder economics. Q2 adjusted EBITDA margin was 59%, adjusted operating margin was 5%, and the GAAP net-loss margin was 24%. CoreWeave is an infrastructure operator rather than a frontier lab, but the example shows how depreciation and financing requirements can separate EBITDA from equity earnings in an asset-intensive business.

The mortgage-market analogy is consequently limited. Standardization can broaden the lender base and reduce transaction costs. It cannot eliminate concentrated customer exposure, hardware obsolescence, deployment risk, or correlated collateral values. Seniority determines contractual priority; repayment still depends on cash generation and recoverable value.

FRONTIER LAB VALUATION: TRAINING ADDBACKS REQUIRE AN ECONOMIC MAINTENANCE TEST

The frontier-lab exhibit is an illustrative financial framework rather than a reported industry income statement. For $100 of revenue, it assumes $20 of inference cost and $20 of operating expenses, producing $60 of EBITDA before training. It then subtracts $60 of training expenditure, leaving no EBITDA, and $50 of capital expenditure, producing negative $50 of free cash flow.

The favorable interpretation is that some training spending creates future capabilities and markets rather than supporting current revenue. Separating that discretionary growth investment from the earnings power of an existing product can be useful. The problem is that training expenditure can be operationally adjustable while remaining economically necessary.

A lab that materially reduces development spending may lose capability, pricing power, customer retention, or the ability to serve emerging workloads. Competitive maintenance can include pretraining, post-training, evaluation, model optimization, safety engineering, and ongoing product development. The relevant normalization removes expenditure that can genuinely be reduced without impairing the revenue and margin assumptions being capitalized.

The slide's own arithmetic illustrates the limitation of the adjustment. Eliminating all $60 of training spending while retaining $50 of capital expenditure produces only $10 of free cash flow before omitted items. A 60% EBITDA margin before training does not imply a 60% cash margin. Interest, taxes, working capital, stock-based compensation, and the treatment of leased versus owned compute require additional reconciliation.

Strong revenue disclosures validate commercial scale without establishing the assumed margins. Anthropic's May financing announcement reported that annualized revenue had exceeded $47 billion and announced a $65 billion funding round at a $965 billion post-money valuation. An annualized revenue figure is different from recognized annual revenue, cash collections, or sustainable free cash flow. The announcement does not validate the hypothetical 80% gross margin or 60% EBITDA margin before training in Coatue's exhibit.

Revenue per GW is useful only with consistent definitions. Comparisons must address purchased versus owned capacity, utilization, hardware generation, training versus inference allocation, and gross versus net revenue recognition. Otherwise, a high ratio can reflect a different business model or accounting perimeter rather than superior underlying productivity.

A rigorous valuation should separate the existing product's sustainable cash generation, the cost and expected value of further capability development, and the option value of new markets. Capitalizing a large adjusted earnings figure while simultaneously assuming continued frontier leadership funded by the excluded expenditure risks overstating value.

SOFTWARE, DISTRIBUTION, AND PRIVATE CAPITAL

The broader software implication is a redistribution of value among interfaces, workflows, data, and execution. Products whose value rests primarily on a user interface or a narrow manual workflow can face pressure as agents interact directly with underlying systems. Businesses controlling difficult-to-replace records, trusted processes, enterprise permissions, or essential infrastructure may retain relevance even as the visible interface changes.

Seat-based models can be exposed if automation reduces the number of human users. Consumption and outcome-based models can benefit from greater task volume, but also introduce variable inference costs and customer scrutiny of unit economics. Revenue growth is therefore insufficient without evidence that pricing captures the value of completed work and covers its delivery cost.

Incumbents also possess advantages that simple disruption baskets can understate. Existing distribution, procurement relationships, governance capabilities, and embedded customer processes can accelerate AI monetization. Microsoft's paid Copilot adoption provides evidence that established platforms can participate directly in the transition. The software debate is consequently better framed around the durability and pricing of specific workflows than a uniform classification of incumbents as losers.

Consumer agents could alter traffic acquisition and transaction discovery across search, commerce, and applications. The precise outcome depends on which entity controls the customer relationship, authenticates actions, supplies product information, executes payment, and handles fulfillment. An agent can capture the interface while relying heavily on existing transaction infrastructure. This creates opportunities for commerce and payment infrastructure alongside the possibility of pressure on traditional discovery models.

Private capital faces a related duration problem. Long holding periods and infrequent valuation marks can coexist with rapidly changing product economics. A contractual claim on an apparently stable software business may become less secure if its pricing, customer count, or terminal relevance changes. Conversely, short-term public volatility can exaggerate the immediate deterioration of a business with durable cash generation.

Financing structures should therefore be matched to the economic life and cash-flow durability of the underlying assets. Buildings, electrical infrastructure, processors, model intellectual property, and customer contracts do not have interchangeable risk characteristics. Flexibility in ownership and financing can create value, but it can also transfer attractive economics away from existing common shareholders.

INVESTMENT IMPLICATIONS AND THE EVIDENCE THAT WILL DETERMINE RETURNS

The best-supported near-term positive exposure is to funded infrastructure demand that is already translating into shipments, utilization, and recognized profit. Memory and server CPU disclosures provide direct evidence of that conversion. The corresponding risk is that current earnings increasingly reflect scarcity pricing and favorable mix, making subsequent supply additions and normalization more important than the continuation of unit growth alone.

For Meta, the consumer-agent opportunity has strategic substance, but the valuation should distinguish user acquisition from retained utility, and retained utility from monetization. The most informative developments are repeat task execution, transaction conversion, contribution margins, and a demonstrable advertising mechanism consistent with the product's data-use commitments. 

For Intel, the principal tests are server shipments, realized pricing, competitive share, manufacturing execution, and consolidated cash generation. Category expansion can support earnings even with share pressure, but the size of the benefit depends on density improvements and the cost of supplying the additional capacity. 

For cloud operators and frontier labs, the decisive measures are incremental gross profit, revenue quality, utilization of newly delivered capacity, sustaining investment, and cash returns after financing. Backlog and annualized revenue provide useful visibility, but neither substitutes for those measures. Improvements in model efficiency are especially valuable when they lower the cost of delivery faster than competition reduces realized pricing.

For infrastructure equity and credit, commissioning schedules, debt amortization, renewal economics, and customer concentration deserve as much attention as headline contract value. The same technological advances that expand AI adoption can weaken the economics of older equipment or reduce the prices customers will pay at renewal. Contractual protection should be evaluated against that possibility.

A sustained bullish outcome requires useful work to expand rapidly enough, and suppliers to retain enough of its economic value, to support the capital installed. A weaker investment outcome does not require AI adoption to fail. It can arise from successful adoption accompanied by price compression, greater capital intensity, dilution, competitive redistribution, or returns accruing primarily to customers.

The central underwriting requirement is therefore growth in normalized cash flow per diluted share after sustaining investment. Coatue's presentation identifies a potentially enormous economic transition. The securities that benefit most will be determined by the durability of their competitive position and the economics of financing that transition, rather than the scale of the transition alone.

Why A Router Is Your Digital Gun and Why It Needs A Digital Second Amendment

By Blake S. Davis
October 7, 2026

TEXAS ALREADY CALLED IT A WEAPON

Texas says the router in your house is a weapon. In its lawsuit against TP-Link, the state calls the company's devices "modern weapons of war."

I agree with the category. A router is the one piece of equipment that decides what enters your home network and what leaves it. That makes it your digital gun, and it is why you have the right to keep it.

Since February, five states have sued the company that, by their own count, sells at least 60 percent of the home routers Americans buy at retail. Washington has put every foreign-made home router on a national-security list. The companies that rent you your connection got exemptions. The fight is over who holds the key to your network, and I intend to keep mine.

THE GATE OF THE DIGITAL HOME

Every device in your house reaches the internet through one box. The router's firewall decides which connections come in, and its settings decide who can see what is plugged in behind it.

There are two ways to have one. You can rent a gateway from your internet provider, and the provider keeps the keys: it sets the firmware, changes the settings remotely and can see the devices behind it. Or you can buy your own, and the provider's view ends at the port where its line plugs in.

The law already treats that port as a border. The federal wiretap-capability statute, CALEA, binds telecommunications carriers and exempts private networks. Behind a router you own, the law builds in no door for anyone. That is a partition, and it belongs to the homeowner.

The Supreme Court said in District of Columbia v. Heller that the home is where the defense of self, family and property matters most. In 2026 the family's bank logins, medical portals, cameras and children's devices all sit behind that one box.

THE GOVERNMENT CALLED IT A WEAPON FIRST

Washington classified the tools of private communication as arms long before Texas did. In the 1990s the State Department ruled that a graduate student's encryption code was a "defense article" on the U.S. Munitions List. He needed a government license to publish it. A federal court held the code was protected speech, and by 2000 the government had loosened the rules. That case was Bernstein v. Department of Justice.

The Supreme Court's own definition fits. Heller relied on a 1773 dictionary that defined arms as "weapons of offence, or armour of defence." A firewall is armor of defense. In Caetano v. Massachusetts the Court held that the right reaches arms that did not exist at the founding, and Heller protects arms in common use for lawful purposes. Few tools in the American home are in more common use than a router.

No court has been asked whether a router is an arm. I am asking. The state of Texas has already answered in its own pleading.

A WEAPON OF WAR, WITH NO WAR DEFINED

Texas calls my router a weapon of war, and Washington has never said what a cyberwar is. In 2016 a Pentagon official told the House Armed Services Committee that a cyber act of war "has not been defined." The Pentagon later told the Senate the call belongs to the President, "case-by-case and fact-specific." That same year Senator Mike Rounds introduced a bill to make the administration define it. A decade later I can find no published definition.

The ambiguity is a choice. A Council on Foreign Relations analysis of the Rounds bill said governments prefer the discretion. Military doctrine speaks of malicious cyber activity "below the level of armed conflict."

That lets the government play both sides. When a state wants to sue a router company or Washington wants to ban one, the box in my living room is a weapon of war. When a citizen asks who is defending his home network, the same hacking is something less than war, and he is on his own.

Pick one. If this is war, the people have the right to keep the arms that defend their homes. If it is not war, stop calling my router a weapon.

WHO IS BEING DISARMED

The router you own is the one under attack. In March the FCC put every foreign-made consumer router on its national-security list, which covers virtually every router sold for the home. Then it started handing out exceptions.

- NCTA, the cable industry's trade group: FCC waiver through June 9, 2027
- AT&T and Verizon: FCC waivers into mid-2027
- Spectrum's hardware suppliers (Askey, Sagemcom, Sercomm, Hitron, Vantiva): federal approvals, most running into 2027 and 2028
- Netgear, ASUS, eero: federal approvals into 2027 and 2028
- TP-Link: no approval. Sued by Texas, Florida, Iowa, Nebraska and Montana

The approvals are listed in Light Reading's tracker. The FCC's stated reason for the cable waiver was "preventing potential disruptions" to broadband for cable customers. Spectrum's own gateways come from contract makers with plants in China, Vietnam and Taiwan. The declared risk gave way to the providers' convenience.

Look at what the providers have done with that trust. Chinese state hackers got into American carriers, Charter reportedly among them, and researchers traced the intrusions to Cisco network equipment. In November 2025 the FCC rescinded its post-breach security ruling for carriers on a 2-1 vote.

In 2026 an extortion group says it took Charter customer data with one phone call to an employee. 4.9 million email addresses are verified, and the group claims 42 million records. As of this writing I can find no enforcement action by any regulator over either breach. Charter closed its $34.5 billion purchase of Cox in August.

WHAT THEY WILL SAY

They will say TP-Link routers ended up in Chinese botnets. Some did. Microsoft reported that TP-Link routers made up most of one password-spraying network. The Justice Department said the botnet behind the Volt Typhoon campaign was built mostly from end-of-life Cisco and Netgear routers. The fix for an unpatched device is a patch. The FCC's own order would have cut patches off in March 2027, and it extended the deadline to 2029 only after acknowledging that blocking updates would leave millions of devices exposed.

They will say the marketing lied. TP-Link advertised a "100% safeguard." If that is deception, the remedy exists and has been used. The FTC charged ASUS in 2016 and D-Link in 2019 over router security claims, and each got years of audits with no fine. Apple told buyers the Mac "doesn't get PC viruses" until 2012, then edited the page. TP-Link faces five state suits, with Texas, Florida and Montana seeking $10,000 per violation.

They will say Chinese law reaches TP-Link. Chinese law reaches every factory in China, and the gateways the providers rent out come from factories in China too. Texas's petition does not name one customer whose data reached China through a TP-Link router. Country-of-origin labels are governed by a federal customs test, and other router makers assemble in Vietnam under that same test.

THE QUESTION TP-LINK SHOULD ASK

@TPLINKUS should ask the government, on the record, what it wants besides money. The government's deals with communications companies have a history of terms the public never sees.

- In 2003, to clear its sale to a foreign buyer, Global Crossing agreed to put security-cleared U.S. citizens in key posts. They were sworn to secrecy about surveillance requests, even from their own board.
- In 2008 the government threatened Yahoo with fines of $250,000 a day to hand over user data. The fight stayed sealed until 2014.
- In 2013 the FBI demanded Lavabit's master encryption key to reach one user. The key would have exposed 410,000. The owner shut the service down.
- A 2022 draft agreement with TikTok would have let federal agencies inspect its servers on short notice and veto its security executives. The public saw it only because Forbes obtained it.

A router company that buys peace with Washington can be handed the same kind of terms, and some of these agreements are confidential by statute. TP-Link has said it will keep working with the Commerce Department. Five state lawsuits raise the price of saying no.

My demand follows from that. Every term of any settlement between any government and any router maker should be published in full. If the answer to "do you want a way in" is no, put it in writing.

A DIGITAL SECOND AMENDMENT

The right of the people to keep and control their own routers shall not be infringed. Here is what I mean by it.

1. The right to own. Any American may buy a router at retail and attach it to any network. Phone customers won that right for their own equipment in the 1968 Carterfone decision. Internet customers need it in statute.

2. The right to control. The owner holds the admin password, picks the firmware and decides who manages the device. No provider or agency manages it remotely without the owner's consent.

3. No compelled back doors. No government may require a way in as a condition of selling a router here, whether by law, license or settlement. CALEA already bars agencies from dictating equipment design to carriers. Home equipment deserves at least that.

4. The right to maintain. No regulator may cut off security updates to equipment already in American homes. The 2029 cutoff should go.

5. Equal treatment and due process. No brand is banned or sued on claims the government will not publish and prove. The router a provider rents out meets the same standard as the router a family buys.

6. The owner's duty. A right carries responsibility. Keep it patched, change the default password, and replace it when the maker stops supporting it.

A gun in the safe protects the house. So does the box on the shelf by the modem. Both belong to the person who lives there. @USNatArchives

SpaceX Wants $40 Billion in Debt – To Buy Nvidia Chips

Let me show you the number that should make every AI investor stop and think.
$85.7 billion.
That’s how much SpaceX raised in its June IPO. Then it borrowed $25 billion in its first bond sale just five days later. Now it wants $40 billion more—to buy Nvidia chips.

Total debt as of June 30: $38.4 billion. Up from $22 billion at the end of 2025.
This isn’t a company financing growth from cash flow anymore. This is a company financing growth from the credit markets. And the credit markets are watching.

The Structure: $10 Billion in Bank Loans, $30 Billion in Bonds
Here’s exactly what SpaceX is asking for.

Bank loans: Approximately $10 billion
Investment-grade debt: Approximately $30 billion
Total: $40 billion
Lead arranger: Apollo Global Management, expected to lead the deal and help sell the debt to investors
Other participants: PIMCO is among a small group of lenders in discussions to fund the deal

Expected close: 2027
Credit rating: BBB—the second-lowest investment-grade rating. That means insurance companies and pension funds can buy the debt, but it’s not top-tier credit
SpaceX didn’t just decide to borrow $40 billion out of nowhere. Its June bond deal carried interest rates ranging from 5.35% to 6.65%, with a weighted average of 5.855%.
That’s the cost of capital in this environment. And it’s not cheap.

Who Is in the Room: Apollo Leading, PIMCO Looking
This isn’t a typical corporate bond deal. It’s a syndicated financing led by one of the biggest alternative asset managers in the world.

Apollo Global Management is expected to lead the deal and help market the debt to a broad range of investors. Apollo isn’t just a lender—it’s a deal architect. The firm specializes in structuring complex financings for companies that need capital but don’t want to tap the public equity markets.
PIMCO, the world’s largest bond fund manager, is among a small group of lenders in discussions to participate. PIMCO’s involvement signals that the debt is being taken seriously by institutional credit investors.

But here’s the caveat: talks are early. A deal can still die.
The Financial Times reported the transaction is expected to close in 2027, but that’s a long timeline. Anything can happen between now and then—rate moves, market volatility, changes in SpaceX’s capital needs.
The fact that this is being structured as a syndicated deal rather than a single-lender arrangement tells you something: the size is too big for one balance sheet. It needs to be distributed. And distribution takes time.

Why It Matters: The AI Buildout Just Entered the Credit Market
Here’s the structural shift that matters more than any single deal.

For two years, the AI buildout was a cash-flow story. Hyperscalers like Microsoft, Google, and Meta were spending billions on chips and data centers—but they were spending from operating cash flow. Their balance sheets could absorb it.

That’s changing.
Oracle said it expects to raise $45 billion to $50 billion during 2026 through a combination of debt and equity to expand Oracle Cloud Infrastructure, citing contracted demand from customers including Meta, Nvidia, and OpenAI.
CoreWeave has built its entire financing model around borrowing against AI infrastructure and customer contracts. In August, it closed a $2.6 billion loan facility backed by customer commitments.
Broadcom is in talks with investors for a potential $60 billion fundraising effort that would see the chipmaker loan money to customers including Anthropic.

And now SpaceX wants $40 billion to buy Nvidia chips.
The pattern is unmistakable: the AI buildout is shifting from the income statement to the balance sheet. Companies that were funding expansion from profits are now funding it from debt. That’s a fundamentally different risk profile.
Neuberger Berman estimated that hyperscaler, data-center, and semiconductor financing had reached roughly $165 billion before the midpoint of 2026.
Morgan Stanley projects AI infrastructure will need $1.5 trillion in financing in the coming years.
That’s not a cash-flow story anymore. That’s a credit-market story.

The Timing: 30-Year Yields Are at a 2002 High
Here’s the part that makes this deal genuinely risky.

The 30-year Treasury yield crossed 5.61% in late September—a level last seen in 2002. The 10-year is above 5.3%. Both are at 24-year highs.
Why does this matter? Because SpaceX is trying to borrow $40 billion in a market where the risk-free rate is the highest it’s been in over two decades.

Every basis point matters. At a 5.855% weighted average interest rate, SpaceX is paying roughly **$2.34 billion per year in interest** on the $40 billion alone. That’s before principal repayment.
And the existing debt is already trading poorly. SpaceX’s bonds maturing in 2056 are trading at about 85 cents on the dollar, with a yield of about 2.27 percentage points above U.S. Treasuries—similar to the level of junk bonds, according to Axios.

That’s a warning sign. The market is already pricing SpaceX’s long-dated debt like it’s riskier than its BBB rating suggests.
Ray Dalio voiced debt bubble concerns on Wednesday—the same day this deal was reported. Rising rates haven’t curtailed hyperscaler appetites, but the market is starting to ask whether the debt can be absorbed.

The Tape: NVDA Is the Seller, SpaceX Is the Buyer
Let’s map the repricing vectors.

Nvidia (NVDA): Trading around $239.24 as of October 6, near its all-time high. Market cap is back above $5.65 trillion. Nvidia is the seller in this transaction. SpaceX is buying the chips. For Nvidia, this is revenue. For SpaceX, it’s debt.
SpaceX (SPCX): Shares are up nearly 16% over the past week, closing at $171.92** per share. The IPO priced at $135. The first post-IPO trades were at $150. The stock was down 2% on Wednesday as the debt news circulated.
The credit market: SpaceX’s existing bonds are trading at distressed levels. The new $40 billion deal will need to be priced at a premium to attract buyers. That means higher interest costs for SpaceX—and higher yields for bond investors willing to take the risk.

Tech analyst Dan Ives called the development a “smart strategic move for the SpaceX buildout because it fuels the flywheel between launch, Starlink, and AI”.
That’s the bull case. The bear case is simpler: if chip demand is financed with debt, a rate spike hits both the stock and the bond.

What Hits Returns: The Rate Sensitivity Problem
Here’s the tradeoff that every investor in this deal needs to understand.

If you own NVDA: The sale is revenue. Nvidia books the order. The chips ship. The cash is collected. Nvidia doesn’t care how SpaceX finances the purchase. But if SpaceX’s financing costs rise, future chip orders could slow. Nvidia’s revenue is downstream of SpaceX’s balance sheet.
If you own SPCX: The debt is a direct claim on cash flow. At 5.855% weighted average, the interest burden is significant. If rates rise further before the deal closes, the cost goes up. If the AI revenue doesn’t materialize as projected, servicing the debt becomes harder.

If you own the bonds: You’re lending money to a company with a BBB rating, in a high-rate environment, to buy depreciating assets—chips that will be obsolete in 3-5 years. The yield of 2.27 percentage points above Treasuries is the compensation for that risk. Whether it’s enough is the question.
The broader market is already repricing. AI infrastructure debt is no longer a niche corner of the credit market. It’s becoming a major asset class. And that means it’s becoming a systemic risk if something goes wrong.

The Bottom Line: Don’t Trade the Rumor Size. Trade Whether the Debt Closes
Let me be clear about what this is and isn’t.

It is not a done deal. Talks are early. Apollo is leading. PIMCO is looking. But the transaction isn’t expected to close until 2027. A lot can change.
It is a signal. The AI buildout has moved from the equity market to the credit market. Companies that were funding expansion from cash flow are now funding it from debt. That’s a structural shift in how this industry finances itself.

It is a rate-sensitivity event. The 30-year yield at 5.61% is the highest since 2002. Borrowing $40 billion in this environment is expensive. If yields move higher before the deal closes, the cost goes up. If yields fall, the cost goes down. The deal is a leveraged bet on rates.

Here’s what I’m watching:
1. Does the deal close? Apollo and PIMCO’s participation is a positive signal. But 2027 is a long way away. Watch for updates on pricing, syndication, and demand.

2. The interest rate on the new debt. SpaceX’s June bonds carried 5.35-6.65%. The new deal will likely price in a similar range—or higher, given the size and the current rate environment. Watch the weighted average.

3. Nvidia’s order book. If SpaceX closes this deal, it’s a $40 billion order for Nvidia. That’s material. But it also sets a precedent for other AI companies to finance chip purchases with debt. Watch for follow-on deals from Oracle, CoreWeave, and others.

4. The credit market’s appetite. Neuberger Berman estimates $165 billion in AI-related financing already. Morgan Stanley says $1.5 trillion is needed. The question isn’t whether the debt can be raised—it’s whether it can be raised at a reasonable cost.

5. Ray Dalio’s warning. The billionaire investor voiced debt bubble concerns the same week this deal was reported. If more voices join that chorus, the credit market could tighten. And that would make SpaceX’s $40 billion more expensive.

Don’t trade the rumor size. Trade whether the debt closes before yields move again.

The AI buildout just left the cash-flow story and entered the credit market. That’s a bigger shift than any single deal. And it’s one that every investor—stock, bond, or otherwise—needs to understand.

Follow for more deep dives on AI infrastructure, credit markets, and the trades that actually matter.

我最近一直在想一件事：OpenAI 是不是开始不务正业了。

DevDay 上发的是 Dots、AgentKit、Apps SDK，全是应用层的东西。GPT-6.1 Astra 因为安全疑虑被取消发布，GPT-6 Cyber 还在预览阶段。真正的旗舰模型，已经很久没有实质更新了。

一家模型公司，最核心的资产就是模型能力。如果这个东西的迭代速度下来了，其他布局再热闹，也是空中楼阁。

但我越想越觉得，OpenAI 不是不想卷模型，是卷模型的钱不够了。

它一年的算力支出，预计到 2030 年要花 2800 亿美元，现在年化收入大概 400 亿。中间的缺口，靠融资填。融资需要故事，故事需要产品，产品需要用户。Dots 和 AgentKit 这些应用层的东西，本质上是在把算力变成收入，让融资故事有数据支撑。

Anthropic 走的是另一条路，死磕企业端 API，营收增速快、亏损收窄，已经在盈利节奏上反超了 OpenAI。OpenAI 的 C 端订阅占收入 65% 以上，免费用户的算力补贴是沉重的成本负担。

但这里有一个更本质的风险。

巨头做模型，不是为了把模型做到最强。谷歌做 Gemini，是为了守住搜索和云。微软做 MAI，是为了降低对 OpenAI 的依赖。Meta 做 Muse，是为了把 AI 塞进社交生态。它们可以接受模型“第二强”，因为赚钱靠的是生态，不是模型本身。

但 OpenAI 不行。它的订阅费和 API 收入，直接取决于模型是不是“最强”。它的商业模型，建立在“最强者通吃”的假设上。

所以真正的问题不是 OpenAI 会不会被巨头在模型能力上超越，是它会不会在商业闭环上被绕过。

谷歌可以接受 Gemini 比 GPT-6 弱一点，只要用户还留在搜索和 Workspace 里。微软可以接受 MAI 差一档，只要它能省下每年付给 OpenAI 的巨额费用。这些巨头不需要赢在模型上，它们只需要赢在场景上。

而 OpenAI 的模型一旦不再是“最强”，订阅就会流失，API 收入就会下滑。这个假设一旦松动，它的护城河就会塌。

模型是发动机，应用是放大器。发动机慢了，放大器再响也没用。

$MSFT $GOOG $META

免责声明：本文纯属个人观点，不构成任何投资建议。

【今日市場重點｜2026-10-08】

今日最重要嘅變化，唔係AI需求突然消失，而係AI建設同時進入通脹及金融市場分析：

AI投資與能源需求可能推高成本；
AI基建相關發債則同政府競逐長期資金，影響term premium及市場收益率。

兩者相關，但唔係同一個加息理由。

【Fed：AI進入通脹及金融條件討論】

CONFIRMED FACT

Fed於10月7日發布9月15至16日FOMC會議紀錄：

• 所有與會者支持加息25點子，政策利率升至3.75%至4.00%。
• 多數與會者認為年底前再加息一次可能合適，但未來決定仍取決於數據。
• Fed職員上調2026至2028年通脹預測，預計2029年回落至2%。
• 部分官員認為AI建設可能令總需求快過總供應，增加中期通脹壓力。
• 少數官員提高中性利率估計；幾位認為目前政策只屬輕微限制性，甚至未算限制性。

市場運作部分亦指出，大量AI基建私人發債正競逐資本，係近期term premium及美債收益率上升因素之一；部分hyperscaler債券因規模大、年期長，息差仍然偏闊。

但Fed並冇話「因為AI企業發債，所以決定加息」。AI發債屬金融條件分析；AI建設對需求及成本嘅影響，先屬通脹與政策討論。

【市場：10月暫停，唔等於周期結束】

截至Reuters約06:50 ET：

• 美國十年債息約5.34%，接近2002年以來高位。
• 10月加息機率約19%。
• 12月前再次加息嘅市場定價約80%。

市場唔係否定再加息，而係押注Fed會先觀察油價、通脹、金融環境同企業盈利。

【美債拍賣：需求強，但融資水平仍高】

昨日US$39bn十年期美債拍賣：

• 得標收益率：5.300%
• Bid-to-cover：2.77倍
• 間接投標者獲配：80.3%
• Primary dealers承接約2.5%

呢組數字顯示拍賣需求強勁，唔係投資者拒絕承接美債。

但亦要分清楚：市場先將收益率推高至約5.3%，先吸引到大量資金。強勁投標有助限制拍賣當刻嘅升幅，唔代表美國政府長期融資成本已經下降。

今日13:00 ET嘅US$22bn三十年債拍賣，會進一步測試超長年期需求。

【晶片收入：AI需求仍然強】

台積電9月未經審計收入：

• NT$511.86bn
• 按月跌0.6%
• 按年升54.6%

第三季收入約NT$1.49tn，按年增加約50%，高過公司原先收入指引上限。

Samsung第三季初步指引：

• 銷售：約KRW195tn
• 營業利潤：約KRW107.4tn
• 上年同期營業利潤：KRW12.17tn

KRW107.4tn雖然非常高，但Samsung全球公告、投資者披露及Reuters均採用相同數字。詳細分部業績及最終結果要等10月29日公布。

OUR ANALYSIS

數據支持AI運算與記憶體需求未斷，但收入增長仍然不能單獨回答自由現金流、客戶集中度、存貨、GPU使用率，以及買家有幾多建設成本依賴外部融資。

【AI融資：報道存在，但尚未完成】

REPORTED / UNCONFIRMED INFORMATION

WSJ報道、Reuters轉述：

• Broadcom據報安排約US$50bn融資。
• SpaceX據報計劃發行US$30bn投資級債券，再籌集US$10bn銀行貸款購買Nvidia晶片。
• Oracle亦據報尋求融資，但未披露金額。

相關安排未有完整條款、最終定價、投資者分配或已提取金額，不能寫成已完成融資。

Nvidia據報持有SpaceX股份，而SpaceX計劃購買Nvidia晶片，形成股權投資與供應商採購嘅交叉關係。呢種關係唔等於違規或「循環融資」，但分析最終需求時，要分開客戶現金流、股東資本及外部借貸。

真正風險門檻係最終票息、貸款息差、抵押品、銀行保留額，以及項目收入能否支付固定融資成本。

【能源與歐洲】

Reuters於歐洲早段報道：

• Brent近月期貨升至每桶US$104以上，升幅接近4%。
• 法國十年債息約4.93%。
• 歐洲銀行股指數跌近2%。
• 日圓約158.22兌一美元。

油價推高短期通脹，政府同企業同時增加債券供應，會提高市場對長期資金嘅需求。

但昨日十年債拍賣亦證明：只要收益率足夠吸引，市場仍然有強勁資金承接美債。

Grialo                           

我们刚刚起步，但已经迈出了坚实的一步！                        

感谢每一位信任和支持 Rialo 的朋友，这只是开始，未来我们会一起走得更远、做得更大！                           

本周开发者活动的项目让我们一起了解一下吧

1⃣Rialink
1. 项目定位

Rialink 是面向 Rialo 生态的去中心化身份协议，主要解决 Web3 钱包地址缺乏身份信息的问题。

目前钱包本身无法证明用户是谁，而 GitHub、Discord、Farcaster 等社交身份又容易被复制或冒用。Rialink希望通过钱包签名验证用户对钱包的所有权，再将经过验证的社交账号与钱包绑定，生成可以被其他应用查询和验证的身份凭证。

目前支持 GitHub、Discord、Farcaster，X 集成正在开发中。

2. 产品流程

用户首先连接钱包，通过签名完成钱包所有权验证，然后绑定对应的社交账号。

验证完成后会生成一张 RL Card，其中包括：

钱包地址

已验证的社交身份

Trust Level

唯一 ID
其他用户可以通过 Card ID 或钱包地址查询相关身份和信任信息。
Demo 中 GitHub 和部分平台连接偶尔出现问题，但 Discord 和其他已支持平台的验证流程基本可以正常运行。
3. 身份安全机制

Rialink的一个核心设计是 一个社交账号只能绑定一个钱包，用于防止身份 Farming、重复绑定和冒充。

身份绑定、修改都需要钱包签名，第三方无法直接修改用户身份。

系统会为身份凭证生成 Proof Hash，如果数据被篡改，Hash 将无法匹配。

如果用户的 GitHub 或其他社交账号被盗，也可以主动解除绑定，解除后的状态会同步到相关第三方应用。

4. 链上实现与路线

目前 Real Link 会将身份状态转换成 Identity Root Hash，然后通过 Memo Transaction 写入 Real 网络。

后续计划包括：

完善身份 Root Hash 上链

为每个绑定账号建立独立链上记录

实现链上 Policy Attestation

最终让第三方应用可以直接根据链上数据和规则验证用户是否满足某项身份或信任条件。
5. 开发者集成
Rialink 不仅面向普通用户，也希望成为其他 Web3 项目的身份基础设施。

目前提供：

REST API

SDK

Embeddable Widget

API Playground
Webhook
开发者可以直接接入身份验证和 Trust Score，不需要自己重新搭建完整的验证系统。

2⃣Merge Pay 

1. 项目定位
Merge Pay 是一个与 GitHub 开源贡献结合的 Bounty 支付工具。

主要解决两个问题：
开源项目 Bounty 发放过程依赖人工，效率较低

Crypto Treasury 管理过程中存在私钥泄露风险
Merge Pay 希望把 GitHub PR、贡献者身份验证、Bounty 条件和链上资金托管连接起来，实现自动结算。

2. Bounty 工作流程

Sponsor 创建 Bounty 后设置相关规则，并将资金存入 Escrow。

Contributor 完成 GitHub PR 后提交 Claim，系统通过 GitHub Numeric User ID 验证贡献者身份。

Sponsor 审核通过后，资金进入结算流程。

如果 PR 满足规定条件，在 Deadline 前完成验证，系统自动付款；如果超过 Deadline 没有满足条件，则按照规则退款给 Sponsor。

3. 技术架构
项目主要由三个部分组成：

Escrow Program：
使用 Rust 编写，负责资金托管和状态转换。

Proof / Verifier：
根据 GitHub PR、CI、Review 等数据生成并验证证明。

Demo 中强调，用户私钥不会发送到后端。

4. Demo 结果

自动付款：成功。

符合条件的 PR 可以触发自动付款，系统会周期性检查 GitHub 状态，并生成公开可验证的支付凭证。

自动退款：未能在 Demo 中正常触发。

不过手动退款流程测试成功。
本次 Demo 基本验证了 GitHub 工作流与链上 Escrow 自动结算之间的连接。

5. 当前限制
目前版本仍属于 Demo / 开发阶段，主要限制包括：

一个 Bounty 暂时只支持一个 Beneficiary
仅支持公开 GitHub Repository

暂不支持多人拆分奖励

暂无 Arbitration

GitHub 状态检查不是实时进行

Deadline 需要预留足够缓冲时间

CI / Review 无法保证代码完全没有 Bug

ここから先は、スイングトレードに興味のある人だけ読んでもらえれば。（実は300株購入の予定がミスで100株購入で、結果的に助かりました）

新高値ブレイク投資の勉強として、今回のnoteの売買を一度整理しておきます。

■① 最初に注目した理由

noteは6月安値1604円から上昇し、8〜9月には3000円台へ。

チャートを見ると、

3140円
↓
3210円
↓
3405円

と過去の高値が上値抵抗になっていました。

特に3405円は大きな節目。

「ここを出来高を伴って突破したら、新しい価格帯へ移る可能性がある」と考えて監視していました。

■② 3140円、3210円を突破

9月後半になると3140円を突破。

さらに3210円も上回り、株価は高値圏を維持。

この時点でかなり強かったのですが、まだ3405円という大きな壁が残っていたので、私は待ちました。

■③ 3405円を一気にブレイク

9/30。

株価は3405円を明確に突破し、一気に3500円台へ。

出来高も増加。

「高値を少し超えただけ」ではなく、

・大きな陽線
・出来高増加
・過去高値3405円突破
・高値圏で推移

と、かなりブレイクらしい形になりました。

ここで3570円で100株購入。

本当は300株買う予定だったのですが、注文を間違えて100株だけでした😂

結果的には、このミスに後で少し助けられることになります。

■④ ブレイク後、一気に4100円へ

購入翌日は3900円台。

さらに翌日は4100円。

3570円の買値から一時+15％前後まで上昇しました。

この時点では、

「3405円の突破は成功した」

と考えていました。

出来高も増え、終値も高値付近。

新高値ブレイク株としてはかなり強い値動きでした。

ただし、ここで問題が1つ。

決算がすぐ目前に迫っていました。

個人的には、決算またぎのリスクはあったけど、賭けにでたところもあります。後悔はしてません。

■⑤ 10/6決算

決算自体はかなり良い内容でした。

3Q累計は、

売上高40.6億円　前年比+33.2％
営業利益8.5億円　+567％
経常利益8.6億円　+514％
純利益9.9億円　+368％

本業もしっかり伸びていて、

note売上 +21.8％
note pro +32.1％

3か月単独でも売上・営業利益ともに高水準。

数字だけを見ると、かなり強い決算でした。

ただし……

通期予想は据え置き。
追加の上方修正はありませんでした。

ここが株の難しいところ。

「良い決算」と
「株価が上がる決算」

は同じではありません。

決算前に株価がすでに大きく上昇していたため、市場にはかなり期待が織り込まれていた可能性があります。

■⑥ 好決算なのに急落

決算翌日。

株価は大幅安。

3405円のブレイクポイントまで一気に戻ってきました。

さらに終値3150円、ストップ安。

しかも出来高を大きく伴った下落。

ここで状況が完全に変わりました。

「決算内容は良い」

でも、

「株価は3405円のブレイクを維持できない」

これは無視できません。

私はnoteを「好決算株」として買ったのではなく、

「新高値ブレイク株」

として買っています。

ならば、ブレイクが崩れたら撤退を考える必要があります。

■⑦ 3130円に逆指値

最後の支持帯として見ていたのが、

3140円前後。

そこで3130円以下になったら成行売却する逆指値を設定。

翌朝、下落が速く、3130円で逆指値が発動。

実際の約定は3060円でした。

買値3570円
売値3060円

100株なので、

損失 約5万1000円
約−14％

で今回の取引は終了。

■今回の反省

まず、3570円で買ったこと自体は、それほど悪い判断だったとは思っていません。

3405円を出来高付きで突破し、その後4100円まで上昇。

少なくともエントリー時点では、ブレイクの条件はかなり揃っていました。

一方で改善したいのは、

「決算前に+15％近く利益が乗った時、どうするか」

という部分。

今回は100株しかなかったので、

一部利確して残りを決算跨ぎ

という方法が使えませんでした。

もし予定通り300株買っていたなら、

決算前に100株程度利益確定
残り200株で決算を見る

という方法も考えられました。

結果論ですが、今後のルール作りには活かせそうです。

そしてもう1つ。

好決算でも株価が下がることは普通にある。

大切なのは、

「会社が良いか」

だけではなく、

「市場がその数字をどう評価したか」

を見ること。

今回のnoteは、

ブレイク成功
↓
急騰
↓
好決算
↓
期待に届かず急落
↓
ブレイク失敗
↓
撤退

という、新高値投資の怖さと面白さを両方経験できた取引でした。

5万円の損失は痛いですが、今回かなり勉強になりました。

次は、

「ブレイクで入るルール」

だけでなく、

「決算前に利益が乗っている時のルール」

まで事前に決めておこうと思います。

株は買い方より、買った後の方が難しいですね😂

I finally baked a long-form audit of “robot scaling laws.”

AI agents did a lot of the digging; I did a lot of checking, rewriting, and arguing with the drafts.

I reviewed 19 public results related to robot scaling. The short version:

scaling curve ✅
scaling law ❌
Here is the evidence funnel:

19 public results reviewed
→ 16 report multi-scale curves
→ 13 keep the main variable and evaluation reasonably controlled
→ 1 tests a held-out loss forecast
→ 0 completes the full loop from fitting loss, to forecasting the next scale, to validating that forecast on real robots from the same model family.

This distinction matters.
In LLM scaling experiments, data volume D is usually measured in tokens. Token count does not tell us how much new information the data contains, but it remains a relatively stable training unit when the tokenizer, data pipeline, and distribution are held fixed.
Robotics does not yet have an equivalent common unit. Different studies use recorded hours, trajectories, frames, action steps, or action tokens. Even the same “one hour” can produce very different training examples under different sampling rates, action representations, chunking schemes, filtering rules, tasks, environments, and embodiments.
The reported objectives and y-axes vary even further: held-out denoising or vector-field MSE, decoded action error, thresholded accuracy, simulated progress, task completion, cycle time, and real-robot success all answer different questions.
A few examples:

— Figure Helix 2.5 provides the only held-out loss forecast I found: the first three Index-data scales are used to predict offline action loss at 8×. But its 9%→56% real-robot result comes from a separate with-vs-without-pretraining experiment, not the endpoints of that loss curve.

— Dyna-2 scales egocentric human video from 1k to 1M hours. Offline acc@0.5 moves from roughly 40% to 47%, while post-trained robot performance rises from 20% to 53% on its normalized metric. Scaling helps, but the public results cannot tell us whether the final 900k hours were worth the cost.

— Xiaomi-Robotics-1 reports that, with a fixed 5B model, increasing UMI data from roughly 2.5k to 20k hours raises mean success from 53% to 75%. At fixed data, moving from 5B to 10B adds only four points, from 75% to 79%. Useful evidence, but the full model × data grid is still missing.

— Sunday ACT-2 shows that a quality-selected 12.5% subset can outperform a uniformly sampled 50% subset. Nominal scale is not enough: data distribution, repetition, and coverage can matter more than another hour of collection.

My current view:

A general law spanning tasks, environments, and embodiments will probably arrive later, because robotics still lacks a shared training and validation distribution.

But deployment may not need to wait for a predictive scaling law. If a system is reliable enough on a concrete task at an acceptable cost, products may arrive before a general law does.

Perhaps robotics is not waiting for a GPT moment, but an iPhone moment: hardware, software, data, and intelligence finally coming together in a product that works reliably in the real world.

Full visual audit, original figures, evidence boundaries, and sources:

https://t.co/F8dBese20H

records.text:
We are open-sourcing the complete decision pipeline behind ResolveSignal, a pay-per-call decision service for autonomous agents running on @arc  Mainnet.
ResolveSignal is not simply an LLM wrapper or an x402 escrow contract.
The core problem we are solving is how an automated agent can safely purchase one actionable decision without starting a conversation, exposing long-term user data, or paying for an incomplete or low-quality answer.
A caller submits a complete machine-readable contract containing:
• the exact target and objective
• measurable success criteria
• current observed state and timestamp
• evidence and its source
• authority and operational constraints
• actions the caller is actually capable of executing
• fixed action parameters
• response cases that distinguish operation completion from real-world goal resolution
• previous attempts and relevant numerical facts
Missing fields are rejected. Empty strings are rejected. “No information” must be declared explicitly with an explanation. Unknown references, duplicate IDs, stale observations, mismatched targets, approval-dependent actions and unverifiable success conditions are blocked before payment.
The accepted request is canonicalized and compiled into a deterministic decision contract.
Jev performs semantic admission before the customer is charged. It evaluates whether the objective, evidence, restrictions and declared capabilities are sufficient for the bounded service.
If Jev rejects the request or is unavailable, ResolveSignal does not issue a payable quote.
Once admitted, the caller receives one x402 v2 exact payment challenge bound to one request, one payer and one deterministic Arc USDC vault.
After payment verification, GPT‑5.4 does not produce unrestricted advice. It must return a typed DecisionIR containing only:
• one declared action ID
• references to supplied evidence
• every applicable authority and constraint reference
• every required success criterion
• an optional cost comparison that trusted code can recalculate
GPT‑5.4 cannot introduce a new tool, parameter, target, source, goal or capability.
A second bounded GPT‑5.4 stage then evaluates exactly four relationships:
• action fit
• evidence relevance
• constraint alignment
• goal alignment
Every relationship must be supported. An unsupported, uncertain, missing or duplicate verdict fails closed.
Trusted code independently checks admissibility, target identity, reference coverage, effect compatibility, numerical comparisons and response-case semantics. It then binds every accepted semantic claim to SHA‑256 hashes of the exact sources used during review.
The final response is rendered from validated caller declarations and fixed templates. Model-authored prose never becomes an executable instruction.
ResolveSignal returns one conditional next action together with:
• its exact declared parameters
• the target it applies to
• its expected effect
• pre-execution authority and freshness checks
• the caller’s success contract
• conditional outcomes for each declared response case
• explicit separation between operation completion and business-goal resolution
ResolveSignal does not claim that it executed the action, independently verified external evidence or observed the final real-world outcome. The calling agent retains execution authority.
Payment is also bound to output quality:
• invalid input is rejected before payment
• Jev rejection happens before payment
• payment verification failure does not start analysis
• invalid GPT‑5.4 output is withheld
• unsupported semantic review is withheld
• analysis timeout triggers the refund path
• failure to deliver the response triggers the refund path
• the exact service fee is released only after the checked response body is delivered
Each request has an isolated call ID, context, payment recipient and lock. Concurrent calls cannot share responses or payment state. An idempotency key cannot create multiple automatic purchases.
After completion or confirmed refund, the request and result context are deleted. Only minimal settlement metadata may remain for reconciliation. Raw customer input, model payloads and result bodies are not retained in terminal receipts.
The open-source repository includes:
• strict request and response schemas
• the Jev admission adapter
• the GPT‑5.4 planning and semantic-checking adapter
• deterministic compiler and source-binding logic

Linear Fitness Subspace in Protein Language Models Enables Sample-Efficient Directed Evolution

1. The paper proposes the Linear Fitness Subspace (LFS) hypothesis: for a fixed wild type, mutation-induced residue-level representation changes inside a frozen protein language model (PLM) contain a compact, assay-specific set of directions where fitness variation becomes approximately linearly accessible from few labeled variants.

2. Key representation choice: instead of mean-pooled embeddings, they use a mutation-local “site-delta” feature δ(s) = h(s)[p] − h(s_wt)[p], isolating the local displacement at the mutated residue and removing most wild-type background signal shared across variants.

3. Empirical support for “linear accessibility”: on 10 ProteinGym core assays, a simple Ridge regressor on site-delta features achieves average Spearman 0.763 versus 0.825 for an MLP, giving a linearity ratio of 0.921; mean-pooled embeddings are much weaker (0.574). This argues the gain is not just “better PLMs,” but specifically the mutation-aware coordinate.

4. Evidence for “low-dimensionality”: performance saturates with only ~5–10 supervised components; they set k = 8 based on a k@95% saturation analysis. The first learned direction often orders variants by fitness, consistent with a small number of fitness-aligned directions dominating the predictive signal.

5. A geometric explanation for why zero-shot PLM scores can fail: zero-shot scoring is treated as a fixed, task-agnostic projection direction in the same site-delta space. They quantify alignment between the zero-shot direction and the supervised LFS direction via cosine similarity; poorer alignment predicts larger gaps between zero-shot and supervised performance (reported correlation r = -0.81).

6. Method contribution: Subspace-Guided Evolutionary Search (SGES). SGES learns an assay-specific LFS from a small initial labeled set (Ninit = 32 under budgeted search), then conducts surrogate modeling, uncertainty estimation, and acquisition directly in the k-dimensional LFS rather than the full PLM space.

7. SGES search loop: generate candidates near the current population, project each candidate into LFS (z = W^T δ), fit a deep ensemble surrogate in the subspace, compute total uncertainty (aleatoric + epistemic from ensemble disagreement), and select candidates with UCB acquisition a(s) = μ(s) + βσ(s). For multi-mutants, it uses an additive aggregation across mutated sites plus Hamming-distance diversity filtering; W is periodically re-estimated during search.
8. Controlled attribution: with matched dimension k = 8 and the same ensemble+UCB pipeline, LFS learned by PLS (fitness-covarying directions) outperforms generic compression baselines—PCA, random projection, and label-shuffled PLS—indicating improvements come from fitness alignment rather than dimensionality reduction alone.

9. Budgeted directed evolution results (ProteinGym): across an 18-assay search-statistics evaluation with budget Bmax = 500, SGES significantly improves AUC of best-so-far trajectory, final best fitness, and Budget-to-Top-5% versus GP-BO, AdaLead, Random Search, and EVOLVEpro (Wilcoxon signed-rank tests reported). In a compact comparison across recent methods, SGES has the best average best fitness (1.471) and best average rank (1.38).

10. Additional findings and limitations: LFS directions show biological plausibility (high-weight residues enriched near known functional sites in BLAT, P53, PTEN) and selective cross-assay similarity (not universal, but more aligned for related assays). An LFS learned from single mutants transfers usefully to multi-mutant benchmarks (average MAE 0.504 vs 1.228 for zero-shot; Pearson 0.508 vs 0.156), but the authors emphasize this captures a strong additive backbone and may miss strong epistasis; calibration quality remains assay-dependent.

📜Paper: https://t.co/TchDg91pfF

Flock: A Negative-Enriched Protein–Protein Interaction Dataset

1. Flock introduces a large-scale, negative-enriched benchmark for protein–protein interaction (PPI) prediction, directly addressing a long-standing bottleneck: the scarcity and unreliability of explicit non-interacting protein pairs used for training and evaluation.

2. Dataset scale: 26,934 positive PPIs and 377,643 negative PPIs (404,577 total pairs) across 34,959 targets. Most negatives come from PDB biological assemblies (368,937), complemented by high-confidence literature negatives (8,706) that survive stringent curation and do not conflict with positive sources.

3. Key novelty: curated negatives mined from scientific literature using an agentic LLM workflow (Claude Sonnet 5), representing the first major negative PPI data update since Negatome v2 (2013-era). The workflow is designed to reduce classic failure modes (wrong UniProt mapping, reagent/tag contamination, family-level overgeneralization, isoform/fragment confusion, and label inversions).

4. Literature-mining pipeline at a glance: Europe PMC search with negation-focused phrases + regex extraction of matched paragraphs; LLM screening to propose candidate non-interactions; deterministic + LLM-assisted UniProt resolution (with abstention when ambiguous); final agentic, evidence-grounded curation against the full paper text (methods retrievable via a local tool), keeping only full-length, directly supported non-interactions.

5. PDB-derived negatives are regenerated and aggregated at the protein level with a conservative rule: a protein pair is emitted as negative only when every supporting chain-pair instance is non-interacting, reducing the risk of labeling a pair negative when another copy/assembly shows contact.

6. Flock also contributes a rigorous evaluation protocol: the Leakage-Free Set (335 targets; 783 positives; 11,203 negatives). It controls for (a) historical training cutoffs used by co-folding models (using Boltz-2’s 2023-06-01 cutoff) and (b) sequence and interface similarity, via interface-aware clustering in both PPI3D and PINDER.

7. Why leakage control matters here: many structure-based interaction models are trained with date-based cutoffs but can still “see” highly similar proteins/interfaces. Flock’s Leakage-Free Set explicitly removes such overlaps and further enforces per-target partner requirements (≥2 positive partners and ≥20 negative partners) to support realistic evaluation.

8. Benchmarking results highlight generalization gaps: ESMFold2 (co-folding) shows a pronounced performance drop from a “Leaked” set to the Leakage-Free Set, while ESMC (protein language model + sparse autoencoder feature approach) shows a smaller drop, indicating comparatively stronger generalization under strict leakage control.

9. The authors argue that previously reported PPI prediction performance can be inflated by (a) random-pair “negatives” that include false negatives and (b) interface/sequence leakage. Flock is positioned as a more challenging and realistic benchmark for both structure-based and language-model-based PPI predictors.
